questions.question: The word 'metaphysics' originally comes from:
options: The ordering of Aristotle's books (the ones 'after the Physics')
questions.rationale: The editors who arranged Aristotle's works placed the first-philosophy volumes after the Physics - 'ta meta ta physika'. The name is bibliographical, not mystical, though the subject matter often outruns physics.

questions.question: Berkeley's idealism is captured by the slogan:
options: Esse est percipi - to be is to be perceived
The self is a bundle of perceptions
questions.rationale: Berkeley held that reality is fundamentally mental: things are ideas in minds, ultimately God's. The bundle theory is Hume's; 'being precedes essence' is Sartre's existentialism.

questions.question: The classic objection to Cartesian dualism is the:
options: Interaction problem - how do immaterial minds move material bodies?
questions.rationale: Descartes split reality into thinking substance and extended substance, but never satisfactorily explained how the ghost steers the machine - the pineal gland 'solution' convinced almost no one. Materialism, idealism and neutral monism each avoid the split by denying one side or both.

questions.question: The medieval problem of universals asks:
options: Whether redness is one shared entity, a resemblance, or a concept
Whether God can make a stone He cannot lift
questions.rationale: Realism (Plato): universals exist independently; nominalism: only similar particulars exist; conceptualism: universals are concepts in minds. It remains the cleanest training ground for ontological method.

questions.question: Locke's memory-criterion and Hume's bundle theory are rival answers to:
questions.rationale: What makes you the same person across years? Locke: psychological continuity via memory. Hume: there is no self over and above a bundle of perceptions - the Buddhist anatta raised by another route. Bodily-continuity theories are the main rival.

questions.question: Newton held that space is an absolute container; the relationist opponent of this view is:
questions.rationale: Leibniz (with Mach and later Einstein sympathising) argued space is nothing but the system of relations among bodies - no container without contained. The Leibniz-Clarke correspondence is the classic duel.

questions.question: Eternalism about time claims:
options: Past, present and future are all equally real - the 'block universe'
Time is an illusion of consciousness
questions.rationale: Eternalism treats the universe as a four-dimensional block; presentism says only now exists. Relativity's relativity-of-simultaneity is often taken to support the block; presentists fight back.

questions.question: Hume's analysis of causation reduces it to:
options: Constant conjunction - we see B-after-A patterns, never a necessary link
The final cause of a thing
questions.rationale: Hume: all we observe is regular succession plus an expectation born of habit. Kant replied that causality is an a priori category; contemporary theories add counterfactual and interventionist glosses.

questions.question: Kripke's necessary a posteriori truths are best illustrated by:
options: 'Water is H2O' - discovered empirically, yet necessarily true
questions.rationale: Once the empirical discovery fixes what water is, the identity holds in every possible world - necessity combined with empirical origin. Naming and Necessity (1980) thereby revived analytic metaphysics.

questions.question: Compatibilism defines free will as:
options: Acting according to one's own reasons without external constraint - consistent with determinism
Random quantum indeterminacy in the brain
questions.rationale: For compatibilists (Hume, Frankfurt), freedom is not exemption from causation but action flowing from your own desires and deliberation - contrast hard determinism (no freedom) and libertarianism (agent causation).
